question.title: Event-Driven Data Processing
question.scenario: A retail application uses an Azure Cosmos DB container to store orders. They want to automatically trigger downstream processing whenever a new order is added, without constantly polling the database.
question.question-text: What Azure feature can enable this reactive pattern?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about a built-in feature of Cosmos DB that streams mutations as they happen — no polling required.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Use Azure Cosmos DB's Change Feed to react to new orders. The change feed lists all changes (inserts and updates) to documents in the order they occur. By using an Azure Function with a Cosmos DB Trigger bound to the change feed, each new order document will automatically invoke the function shortly after it's written.

ul.li: The Cosmos DB change feed ensures ordering within a partition key, so changes for a given partition come out in sequence.
It's effectively an append-only log of changes - you can attach multiple independent consumers for different purposes.
The change feed provides at-least-once delivery semantics - duplicates are possible; design idempotent handlers.

question.title: Securing Application Secrets
question.scenario: You are developing an Azure App Service web application that needs to connect to an Azure SQL Database and a third-party API. These require sensitive credentials. You want to avoid storing secrets in config files or code.
question.question-text: How should the application securely store and access these secrets in Azure?

choices.choice: Store secrets in Azure Key Vault
Store secrets in Azure Blob Storage

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about a centralized, access-controlled vault purpose-built for storing secrets, keys, and certificates in Azure.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Use Azure Key Vault to store all sensitive credentials. Key Vault is a secure, central repository for keys/secrets/certificates. Configure your Azure App Service to integrate with Key Vault, either using a Managed Identity to fetch secrets or using the Key Vault references feature in Azure App Service configuration. The actual secret values are never in plain text in application settings or code.

ul.li: Use a Managed Identity for the App Service to access Key Vault - this eliminates the need to use any credentials even for Key Vault access.
Key Vault provides secret rotation and integration - update secrets in Key Vault once without redeploying the app.
Key Vault secrets are encrypted with HSMs and only accessible to authorized identities.

question.title: Accessing Azure Resources Without Credentials
question.scenario: A new Azure Function app needs to read from an Azure Storage account and write to an Azure Cosmos DB, but you want no hard-coded keys or passwords in your function code or configuration.
question.question-text: What Azure feature can you use to give the function app authenticated access to these resources?

choices.choice: Store connection strings in app settings

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: What Azure feature gives a resource its own identity in Azure AD so it can authenticate to other services without storing any credentials?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Enable a Managed Identity on the Azure Function and use Azure AD-based access control for the other resources. With a managed identity, the function gets an identity in Azure AD automatically. Assign this identity appropriate access roles (e.g., Storage Blob Data Reader/Writer, Cosmos DB Data Contributor). Inside the function code, use Azure SDKs that leverage the Managed Identity to obtain OAuth tokens silently.

ul.li: The function can request a token by calling the local Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) endpoint - no human or code ever sees a password.
Microsoft takes care of rotating the underlying credentials of the identity, eliminating secret management overhead.
Managed identities can be system-assigned (one per resource) or user-assigned (a standalone identity attached to many resources).

question.title: User Authentication for a Web Application

Enable advanced security like Conditional Access and MFA without changing the app - configured in Azure AD.

question.title: Function Execution Model
question.scenario: A function processes files uploaded to Blob Storage. Some files are large and processing can take several minutes.
question.question-text: What considerations must you make regarding Azure Functions execution limits, and which hosting plan should you choose?

choices.choice: Premium plan or Dedicated plan for longer execution
Process files synchronously in App Service

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The default serverless plan has a short execution timeout. What happens when processing exceeds it, and which hosting tier removes that constraint?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Consumption plan has a default timeout of 5 minutes (configurable up to 10 minutes). For functions that process large files taking several minutes, use the Premium plan (which allows longer timeouts up to unbounded with configuration) or a Dedicated (App Service) plan. Premium also provides pre-warmed instances to avoid cold starts.

ul.li: Premium plan supports VNET integration, larger instance sizes, and no cold start due to always-warm instances.
For truly long-running work, consider Durable Functions which checkpoint progress.
Monitor execution time and consider breaking work into smaller chunks if possible.

question.title: Scaling Azure Functions
question.scenario: An HTTP-triggered Azure Function experiences sudden spikes in traffic during business hours.
question.question-text: How does Azure Functions automatically scale on the Consumption plan, and what factors influence the number of instances?

choices.choice: Automatic scale-out based on incoming event rate and queue length
Scale based on time of day only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about what triggers the platform to add or remove function instances. Is it manual, time-based, or driven by incoming workload signals?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Functions on Consumption plan uses a scale controller that monitors the rate of events and determines when to add or remove instances. For HTTP triggers, it scales based on request rate. For queue triggers, it considers queue length and message age. Scale-out is automatic and can happen rapidly during traffic spikes.

ul.li: The scale controller is trigger-specific - each trigger type has its own scaling logic.
There's a maximum instance limit (default 200 for Consumption, configurable).
Cold starts can occur when scaling out; Premium plan mitigates this with pre-warmed instances.

ul.li: Durable timers use Azure Storage for state - they survive restarts and scale events.
Timers can be canceled using CancellationToken for timeout patterns.
For recurring schedules, use timer triggers; for workflow waits, use durable timers.

question.title: Data Encryption Requirements
question.scenario: Sensitive customer data is stored in Azure Storage and Azure SQL Database. Regulatory compliance requires encryption.
question.question-text: What encryption mechanisms does Azure provide by default?

choices.choice: Encryption at rest by default; TLS in transit

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Does Azure require you to opt in to encryption, or is data protected by default? Think about both data at rest and data in transit.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure provides encryption at rest by default for Storage (SSE) and SQL Database (TDE) using Microsoft-managed keys. All data in transit uses TLS 1.2+. For additional control, use customer-managed keys (CMK) stored in Key Vault. SQL Database also supports Always Encrypted for sensitive columns.

ul.li: CMK with Key Vault gives you control over key rotation and can meet compliance requirements.
SQL Always Encrypted protects data even from DBAs - only client with key can decrypt.
For defense in depth, combine encryption at rest, in transit, and client-side encryption where needed.

question.title: Managed Identity Scope
question.scenario: A single managed identity is used by multiple applications to access Azure resources.
question.question-text: What are the tradeoffs between using a system-assigned versus a user-assigned managed identity in this scenario?

choices.choice: User-assigned is better for sharing across multiple resources; system-assigned is tied to one resource

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: One identity type lives and dies with its resource; the other is a standalone object shareable across many resources. Which fits a multi-app scenario better?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: System-assigned identity is created for and tied to a single Azure resource - deleted when the resource is deleted. User-assigned identity is a standalone Azure resource that can be attached to multiple applications. For least privilege, user-assigned allows centralized permission management for a group of apps with similar access needs.

ul.li: User-assigned identities persist independently - useful for blue-green deployments or resource recreation.
A resource can have both system-assigned and multiple user-assigned identities.
For single-use resources, system-assigned is simpler; for shared access patterns, user-assigned provides better management.

question.title: Graceful Shutdown Handling
question.scenario: An App Service instance is being scaled down while processing requests. You need to ensure in-flight work is completed.
question.question-text: How should the application be designed to shut down gracefully?

choices.choice: Handle application stopping events and complete in-flight work

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When the platform signals shutdown, the app has a grace period. What should it do during that window to avoid dropping in-flight work?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Implement graceful shutdown: listen for shutdown signals (SIGTERM, IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping), stop accepting new requests, complete in-flight operations, and flush any buffered data. App Service provides a configurable shutdown timeout (default 90 seconds for Windows). For long-running operations, consider checkpointing progress to resume elsewhere.

ul.li: Use CancellationToken propagation to signal in-flight operations to complete quickly.
For message processing, don't complete/delete messages until processing is truly done.
Consider using Durable Functions for long-running work that can checkpoint and resume on any instance.
